clinicalScope: Bone marrow failure (pancytopenia) in adult patients in low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Bone Marrow Failure
subject: Medicine
summary: Bone marrow failure is when the marrow cannot make enough blood cells, leading to fatigue, infections and bleeding. In East Africa, infections, nutritional deficiencies and inherited disorders are common causes.

sections.p: Bone marrow failure refers to inadequate production of one or more blood cell lines, resulting in anemia, neutropenia and/or thrombocytopenia.

t.b: Low Hb, ANC, platelets indicate marrow failure

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections and nutritional deficiencies dominate.
b: Infections: HIV, malaria, disseminated TB, hepatitis B/C
Nutritional: severe vitamin B12/folate, copper deficiency
Inherited: sickle‑cell aplastic crisis, Fanconi anaemia

t.b: Positive indicates need for ART and possible opportunistic infections

sections.p: The marrow micro‑environment (stromal cells, macrophages, sinusoids) fails to support progenitor proliferation.
b: Infections trigger cytokine‑mediated apoptosis of progenitors
Nutrient deficiencies impair DNA synthesis in erythroid and myeloid lines
Inherited defects disrupt DNA repair or ribosomal function

sections.p: Symptoms reflect the lowest cell line and the underlying cause.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Ask about infections, medications, diet, family history, and bleeding.
b: Recent fevers, night sweats, weight loss – infection clues
Use of herbal remedies or benzene exposure – toxins
Family history of blood disorders – inherited causes

t.b: Can be done with a simple microscope

sections.p: Differentiate marrow failure from peripheral destruction or sequestration.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use the most available tests to confirm marrow failure and identify cause.
b: Serum ferritin, B12, folate – nutritional status

sections.p: Classify by cytopenia severity to guide urgency of treatment.
Co‑existing conditions can mask or worsen marrow failure.
b: Anemia of chronic disease – low iron but normal ferritin

sections.p: Treat underlying cause, support blood counts, and monitor.
b: Infections: broad‑spectrum antibiotics for neutropenic fever; ART for HIV; anti‑TB drugs for TB
Transfusions: packed cells if Hb <7 g/dL; platelets if <20×10⁹/L with bleeding
Growth factors: filgrastim if available for severe neutropenia

t.b: Use ceftriaxone + gentamicin if local resistance patterns

sections.p: Severe cytopenias can lead to life‑threatening events.

b: Elderly – higher risk of infections and drug toxicity

sections.p: Depends on cause and response to treatment.
Certain tests may be falsely normal or abnormal in low‑resource settings.
b: Serum ferritin ↑ in infection – may mask iron deficiency
Peripheral smear quality depends on technician skill
Rapid HIV tests may miss early infection

whenToSeekHelp: Severe neutropenia with fever (ANC <0.2×10⁹/L), bleeding with platelets <10×10⁹/L, signs of sepsis, severe anemia (Hb <4 g/dL)

faq.q: What is the most common cause of bone marrow failure in East Africa?
faq.a: Infections such as HIV, malaria, and tuberculosis are the leading causes.
Yes, vitamin B12, folate and copper deficiencies respond rapidly to supplementation.

faq.q: When is a bone marrow aspirate necessary?
faq.a: When cytopenias are unexplained after basic work‑up or when myelodysplasia is suspected.

exam: What is the first step in managing a patient with ANC <0.2×10⁹/L and fever? — Start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics and monitor vitals.
How does HIV infection lead to bone marrow failure? — Chronic immune activation and opportunistic infections cause cytokine‑mediated apoptosis of progenitors.
Why is a peripheral smear important in suspected marrow failure? — It reveals morphology suggestive of nutritional deficiencies or dysplasia.
When should filgrastim be considered? — Severe neutropenia (ANC <0.5×10⁹/L) with ongoing infection or before invasive procedures.
What red flag indicates risk of intracranial haemorrhage? — Platelets <10×10⁹/L or active bleeding.
How would you differentiate aplastic crisis in sickle‑cell disease from other causes of anemia? — Look for sudden drop in Hb, reticulocytosis, and recent parvovirus B19 exposure.
What is the significance of a normal ferritin in a patient with anemia? — It suggests anemia of chronic disease rather than iron deficiency.
Why avoid chloramphenicol in low‑resource settings? — It can cause aplastic anaemia, a serious complication.
What supportive care is indicated for Hb <7 g/dL? — Packed red cell transfusion and monitoring for volume overload.
How does hypersplenism present differently from marrow failure? — Splenomegaly with normal marrow cellularity and often normal peripheral counts.
